intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that osteogenesis imperfecta type XIII (OI13) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the BMP1 gene on chromosome 8p21.3.

checks.claim: Osteogenesis imperfecta type XIII (OI13) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the BMP1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: we report the identification of a homozygous missense mutation in a highly conserved residue of the protease domain of BMP1/mTLD in two siblings diagnosed with AR-OI type III
checks.explanation: Paper reports only a homozygous mutation; compound heterozygous mutations and the OI13 designation are not addressed.

checks.claim: The BMP1 gene is located on chromosome 8p21.3.
checks.evidence_quote: BMP1 and its longer isoform mammalian Tolloid protein (mTLD) are alternative spliced products of BMP1 (MIM# 112264), which is located on 8p21.3.

paragraphs.text: Osteogenesis imperfecta type XIII (OI13) is an autosomal recessive bone fragility disorder with recurrent fractures. Martínez-Glez et al. (2012) and Cho et al. (2015) described a severe form with bone deformities, umbilical hernia, short stature and delayed motor development. Bone mineral density has been reported as decreased (Martínez-Glez et al., 2012), normal (Valencia et al., 2014) or increased (Asharani et al., 2012; Fahiminiya et al., 2015). Fahiminiya et al. (2015) described a form with mainly lower extremity fractures and a mineralization defect in bone tissue.

checks.explanation: Paper describes severe deformities, large umbilical hernia, very low length SD, and delayed motor development.

paragraphs.text: Munns et al. (2004) described 3 unrelated children with an apparently new bone fragility disorder associated with an idiopathic mineralization defect. Recurrent lower limb fractures began with weight bearing. The patients had none of the phenotypic, radiologic or histomorphometric features typical of osteogenesis imperfecta, idiopathic juvenile osteoporosis or mild autosomal dominant osteopetrosis. Radiographs showed increased metaphyseal trabeculation and normal to increased cortical thickness, with no evidence of rickets or osteomalacia. Areal and volumetric bone mineral density of the lumbar spine showed no major change. Iliac bone biopsies showed a paucity of the birefringent pattern of normal lamellar bone. Histomorphometry showed osteomalacia, with a prolonged mineralization lag time and a decreased mineral apposition rate. Calcium and phosphate metabolism was normal, and type I collagen mutation analysis was negative.

paragraphs.text: Martínez-Glez et al. (2012) studied 2 sibs born to Egyptian parents who were first cousins. The 15-year-old female proband had a tibial fracture at birth and then had 10 to 15 spontaneous fractures per year. She had a triangular face, broad forehead, wide palpebral fissures, long eyelashes, faint blue sclerae, long philtrum, thin lips and prominent ears. She had a large umbilical hernia, generalized hypotonia, muscle wasting and hirsutism. Gross motor development was delayed, and she could not stand unsupported. Mental development was normal, and dentinogenesis imperfecta was absent. She had severe generalized bone deformities, arachnodactyly, hyperextensible elbow, wrist and interphalangeal joints, kyphoscoliosis and pectus carinatum. Radiographs showed multiple fractures, lack of bone modeling, serpentine thin tibiae and fibulae, platyspondyly, wormian bones and generally decreased bone density. At 13 years, weight was -3.8 SD, length -11.5 SD and head circumference -3.0 SD. Her 5-year-old brother had femoral bowing detected on prenatal ultrasound and fractures of both femora at birth, followed by about 15 fractures per year. His findings were similar to his sister's, including a large umbilical hernia. He also had a wide symphysis pubis, with length -7.2 SD and a normal head circumference. In both sibs, serum calcium and phosphate were normal and alkaline phosphatase was slightly high. Both were diagnosed with OI Sillence type III, one of the groups defined by Sillence et al. (1979).

paragraphs.text: In 2 Egyptian sibs with OI13, born to consanguineous parents, Martínez-Glez et al. (2012) found a homozygous c.747C-G transversion in exon 6 of the BMP1 gene, causing a phe249-to-leu (F249L) substitution. The mutation was found by sequencing BMP1 within a region of shared homozygosity and segregated with the disease. It was absent from 100 control chromosomes of the same ethnic origin and 884 European control chromosomes. Phe249 lies in the protease domain and is conserved in all members of the astacin family of metalloproteases. Patient fibroblasts showed impaired C-terminal processing of procollagen type I, with less pN-alpha-1(I) and free C-propeptide, although some residual activity remained. Overexpressing wildtype mTLD (the longer BMP1 isoform) in NIH3T3 cells and human fibroblasts increased C-propeptide cleavage, but overexpressing the mutant did not.

paragraphs.text: In a patient with OI and normal bone density, Valencia et al. (2014) found the homozygous c.34G-C mutation in the BMP1 gene, which had been reported before. paragraphs.text: Fahiminiya et al. (2015) performed whole-exome sequencing in 4 unrelated children with a bone fragility disorder involving mainly lower extremity fractures and a bone mineralization defect. Three were homozygous for a c.*241T-C change in BMP1, affecting the polyadenylation signal of the transcript for the short isoform, BMP1-1. Their skin fibroblasts had low levels of BMP1-1 transcript and protein. The fourth child was compound heterozygous for c.*241T-C and a c.2107G-C change in exon 15, which affected splicing of both BMP1-1 and the long isoform, BMP1-3. In both genotypes, skin fibroblast supernatants contained less free procollagen type I C-propeptide than controls. The authors concluded that isolated lack of BMP1-1 causes bone fragility in children.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sibs with severe OI13 born to consanguineous Egyptian parents, Martínez-Glez et al. (2012) found a homozygous c.747C-G transversion in exon 6 of the BMP1 gene, causing a phe249-to-leu (F249L) substitution. The residue lies in the protease domain and is conserved across the astacin family of metalloproteases. The parents and 2 unaffected sibs were heterozygous. Overexpressed mutant mTLD did not increase C-propeptide cleavage, whereas wildtype mTLD did.
